articleSummary: At the ERS 2026 congress, experts urge rethinking ICU care for deadly viral infections after concurrent Andes hantavirus and Bundibugyo Ebola outbreaks. Genomic sequencing linked isolates to South American strains, supporting a single zoonotic spillover in Argentina followed by limited human-to-human spread on board; over 317 high‑risk contacts in 33 countries were quarantined for 42 days, with the outbreak declared finished on 2 July 2026. Separately, Bundibugyo Ebola virus caused >4,000 confirmed cases and >2,000 deaths in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Uganda, presenting early symptoms like headache, vomiting, myalgias, and diarrhea; hemorrhagic symptoms were uncommon, and nosocomial spread worsened the crisis amid distrust in public health messaging. The report emphasizes distinguishing viral sepsis from bacterial sepsis and the need for rapid international cooperation, clear public communication, testing, and virus-specific spokespersons.

articleHeadline: India's Rabies Crisis: Urgent Need for Coordinated Canine Vaccination
articleSummary: Rabies in India remains a canine-transmitted public health crisis with the nation at risk of missing the WHO 2030 target to eliminate human rabies. Within states, vaccination coverage and surveillance are uneven, reflecting a gap between national policy and ground-level execution. Chile (rabies-free by WHO in 2019) and Bhutan (rabies-free by 2021) illustrate success through mass canine vaccination, strict stray-dog management, and robust surveillance. Experts warn that fragmented interventions must give way to a coordinated national strategy to reach the 2030 global target. Required reforms include strengthening veterinary services, securing consistent funding for anti-rabies programmes, and intensifying public awareness to prevent bites. Central government recognizes coordination with states, but incremental changes are deemed insufficient for rapid, comprehensive reform.

articleHeadline: Genetically modified bacteria create protective shield against Salmonella attacks
articleSummary: Engineered nonpathogenic E. coli delivering a Salmonella-specific phage protected mice from oral Salmonella infection in Nature Microbiology. The team, led by Bryan Hsu and Rogerio Bataglioli, created a 'lytic phage-producing lysogen' (lyto-lysogen): an E. coli host carrying a phage that infects Salmonella and, once released in the gut, lyses the pathogen, rapidly increasing antipathogen phages and eradicating the infection. Salmonella is a high-burden, antibiotic-resistant pathogen prioritized by the CDC, motivating alternative tools beyond antibiotics. Phage therapy in the gut is hard due to phage-bacteria coexistence and limited access to pathogens; the researchers disguised the phage by introducing a Salmonella gene into the E. coli genome, so Salmonella treats it as self. The approach could be adapted to other bacteria. Bataglioli plans further work at the State University of Campinas, São Paulo, Brazil; supported by NIH and PhRMA Foundation.

articleSummary: Two residents of Frankfurt’s Schwanheim district have malaria, likely from an imported Anopheles mosquito linked to the airport. They did not work at the airport nor recently travel to malaria-risk areas. In July, six airport employees were infected, two of whom died. Laboratory confirmation led to the health department notification. Airport malaria occurs when infected Anopheles mosquitoes from tropical regions reach Germany by plane or cargo and bite people; such cases are rare; the last Frankfurt airport case before this cluster was in 2023. Risk in Schwanheim is low; the cases are about five kilometers from the airport. Mosquitoes collected around the airport and the patients’ homes were sent to Antwerp Tropeninstituut for genetic analysis; no Anopheles mosquitoes have been found yet. Incubation is 7-15 days; transmission by local mosquitoes is theoretically possible but unlikely; climate change and higher flight traffic from Cameroon, Ghana, and Nigeria could increase future cases.

articleSummary: El Niño-linked Pacific warming could raise dengue risk in Kerala, IITM Pune-led study finds. Kerala recorded 7,188 confirmed dengue cases between June and August, about 60% above the decade-average. Analyzing 2006–2019 data, researchers link El Niño years with higher Kerala dengue incidence, as warmer Pacific waters create warmer, drier pre-monsoon conditions conducive to Aedes breeding before monsoon. Lead times peak about three months for sea-surface temperatures; including humidity and temperature extends to nearly five months, enabling earlier vector control and hospital preparedness. Influenza A, one of four influenza virus types (A, B, C, D) that infect humans, includes subtypes A(H1N1) and A(H3N2). By contrast, the common cold is caused by more than 200 respiratory viruses (often rhinovirus) and typically presents milder, slower-onset symptoms such as runny nose, congestion, sneezing, sore throat, and cough; fever is less common in adults. Influenza usually begins abruptly with fever, body aches, cough, headache, and fatigue, and fever plus cough can strengthen suspicion; a BMJ study notes fever as a helpful sign and cough has high sensitivity (~92%). Because symptoms overlap, laboratory testing is often needed to confirm influenza vs. other respiratory infections; severe illness risk remains for high-risk groups.
